title: Talking to Your Computer: The Terminal

intro.text: As a manager of an AI coding assistant, you won't write the code — but you will need to work in the place where the AI actually operates: the terminal. It's where you'll launch Claude Code, watch what it does, and run the quick checks that tell you whether the work was done right. This chapter takes you from “what is that black window?” to confidently creating, exploring, and verifying folders from the command line on your own machine.

intro.title: Before you continue
intro.text: Lessons 1.2 and 1.3 cover the same skills on different operating systems. Work through the one that matches your laptop — you only need one of them. Commands differ slightly between Windows and macOS, so follow the lesson for your OS.

lessons.title: The CLI and the Terminal
lessons.objective: Understand GUI, CLI, and the terminal so you can use and supervise an AI coding agent.

steps.title: There are two ways to use a computer

blocks.text: Today we mostly control computers through a graphical screen: right-click to make a new folder, double-click to open it, drag a file to move it. It feels so natural that we forget it isn't the only way to talk to a computer.

That familiar way of working. You click icons you can see on the screen and drag files into folders — a graphics-based interface. Because you operate the computer with a mouse and graphics, it's called a Graphical User Interface — GUI for short. You just press what you see, so it's intuitive: anyone can pick it up in minutes.

blocks.alt: A graphical interface uses windows, icons, and buttons.
blocks.caption: A graphical interface uses windows, icons, and buttons.

blocks.text: Point, click, and drag what you can see — that's a GUI (Graphical User Interface).

The complete opposite. Almost no mouse, almost no graphics. A dark window with a blinking cursor, where you type commands on the keyboard to make the computer do things. Because you drive the computer with lines of commands, it's called a Command Line Interface — CLI for short.

blocks.alt: A text-based interface receives typed commands.
blocks.caption: A text-based interface receives typed commands.

blocks.text: Typing commands to talk to the computer — that's the CLI (Command Line Interface).

“Who still types commands in this day and age?” you might wonder. But the CLI is alive and well — it's still the main way developers work. Think of it like ordering food: tapping through the menu on a McDonald's self-order kiosk is the GUI; walking up to the counter and telling the cashier exactly what you want is the CLI.
“Almost every developer tool you'll use in this course — including Claude Code — runs in the CLI.”
blocks.title: Another way to think about it

blocks.text: That's why anyone managing AI-built software needs to be comfortable with the basics of the CLI. The AI does its work here, and this is where you'll watch it work, spot when something looks off, and run your own checks instead of taking the AI's word for it.
A terminal is simply the program that gives you a place to type those commands. It comes pre-installed on every computer — there's nothing to download.
Click the Search box in the taskbar.
Click Windows PowerShell to launch it.
Windows — search for PowerShell in the taskbar and run it.
Press Cmd + Space to open Spotlight.

lessons.title: Terminal Basics — Windows
lessons.objective: Learn the core PowerShell commands well enough to verify with your own eyes what an AI assistant has created, moved, or deleted on Windows.

blocks.text: Type powershell (or terminal) into the Windows search box and launch it. The path you see right away — something like C:\Users\yourname — is your current working directory: the folder your commands will run in. This matters for a manager: when the AI creates files, they land relative to a working directory, and this is how you confirm you're looking in the right place.
“A ‘directory’ is just another word for a folder.”

lessons.title: Terminal Shortcuts Worth Knowing
lessons.objective: Pick up the three keyboard shortcuts that make working in the terminal fast: recalling the previous command, wiping a mistyped line, and deleting word by word.

blocks.text: Press the up-arrow key (↑) and the command you just ran is pulled right back onto the line, ready to run or edit.
P.S. Extremely handy when you need to run the same command several times in a row — like re-running a version check after a fix.
